expectations.text: Defines JWT in plain words (a signed token carrying claims / JSON Web Token) in the same sentence it first appears

expectations.text: Defines 'stateless' in plain words (the server keeps no per-session record) the first time it is used
expectations.evidence: First use is immediately explained in the same sentence/paragraph: "That last step is where "stateless" comes from." ... "so any server that knows the verification key can authenticate a request without checking anywhere else first."

expectations.text: Answers the 'you can't log someone out' premise as partly true with conditions, rather than a flat yes or no
expectations.evidence: States both sides explicitly and adjacently: "it's accurate that a plain JWT can't be revoked through the JWT mechanism alone. What's overstated is treating that as" [the broader claim]. Closed out with: "The accurate version of what you heard is less "JWTs can't be logged out" and more "a bare JWT has no revocation built in, so you add a little state back for the parts that need it.""

expectations.text: States the limit of the stateless model: server-side revocation needs some state, naming at least one concrete option (denylist/blocklist, short expiry with refresh tokens, or rotating a signing key)
expectations.evidence: States "What ships is JWTs plus a small, deliberate amount of state, just enough to support revocation" and names a concrete option: "Keep a small revocation list, for instance a Redis set of token IDs using the `jti` claim, and check it on every request."
